assumptions: That the 13:34:00Z deploy is related to the slowdown at all — this rests only on timing, not on any evidence tying the released code to the observed latency.

That the change record is complete: the conclusion 'the only change in six weeks' assumes nothing (config edits, feature-flag toggles, dependency deploys) happened outside the systems the investigation could read.
That the service genuinely recovered rather than the alert clearing for another reason; no post-recovery health check was performed.

Peak latency and error figures cited during the investigation (p95 220ms to 5000ms, errors to 12%) come from the investigator's narrative reading of a handful of sparse log lines and were not independently verified; they are not the incident's measured impact.
That a rollback would have helped — this was never tested, since no mitigation was executed.
input.executive_summary:
For roughly two and a half minutes early on 12 September 2026, one backend service became very slow and a fraction of requests to it failed outright instead of completing. Users of features depending on that service would have seen slow responses and some errors or timeouts during that window; the impact was confined to that service and ended when it returned to normal on its own.

Nothing was changed or fixed in response. The automated responder investigated, repeatedly settled on a code release made about three minutes before the slowdown as the likely trigger, and proposed rolling it back — but the rollback was not carried out because the automation was not permitted to take that action, and no alternative safe action was available. The service recovered by itself while the incident was being handed to a human, so the cause remains unproven and no evidence exists that anything anyone did ended the incident.

Because the trigger was never confirmed and the suspect release is still in production, the same failure can recur. Follow-up should be a human review of that release's contents alongside the service's dependency and datastore behaviour during the window, and a decision on whether rollback should be an action the automation is allowed to take.
input.root_cause: Undetermined. The only change on record for io-shop in the preceding six weeks was the deploy of revision 9f4c1e7b2a3d5c8e1f0b6a4d2c9e7b5a3f1d8c6e at 13:34:00Z, landing in the last healthy minute before p95 latency began climbing and requests began timing out, so a latency regression introduced by that deploy is the leading suspect — but the correlation is purely temporal. The logs read during the incident are generic latency and timeout lines that name no subsystem, dependency, query or flag, no rollback or any other action was ever executed (every proposed mitigation was rejected at the tier gate as not reversible), and the service recovered on its own at the moment of escalation, so nothing confirmed or refuted the deploy hypothesis. A downstream dependency or resource stall remains a live alternative, supported by the fact that request volume fell slightly while latency rose sharply.
